The list she compiled when she was just fourteen—I recall being so impressed by her discernment that I kept it for a while; and I daresay she has produced an even better one now. But I have given up on expecting Emma to follow any regular course of reading. She will never submit to anything that demands diligence and perseverance, or that requires the imagination to yield to reason. Where Miss Taylor failed to inspire, I can confidently say that Harriet Smith will achieve nothing.—You could never persuade her to read as much as you desired.—You know you could not.”

“‘I dare say,’ replied Mrs. Weston, with a smile, ‘that I thought so _then_;—but since we have parted, I can never recall Emma failing to do anything I wished.’”

“There is little point in trying to revive such a memory as _that_,” said Mr. Knightley, feelingly; and for a moment or two he was silent. “But I,” he soon added, “who have had no such enchantment over my senses, must still see, hear, and remember. Emma is spoiled by being the cleverest in her family. At ten years old, she had the misfortune of being able to answer questions that baffled her sister at seventeen. She was always quick and confident: Isabella slow and uncertain. And ever since she was twelve, Emma has ruled the household and all of you. In her mother, she lost the only person capable of managing her. She inherits her mother’s talents, and must have been under her control.”

“I should have been sorry, Mr. Knightley, to rely on _your_ recommendation, had I left Mr. Woodhouse’s family and needed another position; I do not think you would have spoken kindly of me to anyone. I am certain you always thought me unfit for the role I held.”

“Yes,” he said, smiling. “You are better suited _here_; very fit for a wife, but not at all for a governess. But you were preparing yourself to be an excellent wife all the time you were at Hartfield. You might not have given Emma the thorough education your abilities seemed to promise; but you were receiving a very good education from _her_, on the essential matrimonial matter of yielding your own will, and doing as you were told; and if Weston had asked me to recommend him a wife, I should certainly have named Miss Taylor.”

“Thank you. There will be very little merit in making a good wife to such a man as Mr. Weston.”

“Why, to be honest, I am afraid you are rather wasted, and that with every inclination to endure, there will be nothing to endure. We will not despair, however. Weston may grow cross from the indulgence of ease, or his son may plague him.”

“I hope not _that_.—It is not likely. No, Mr. Knightley, do not predict trouble from that quarter.”

“Not I, indeed. I only mention possibilities. I do not claim Emma’s genius for predicting and guessing. I hope, with all my heart, the young man may be a Weston in merit, and a Churchill in fortune.—But Harriet Smith—I have not half finished speaking of Harriet Smith. I think her the very worst sort of companion that Emma could possibly have.

old_rewritten_text:
And is she, at seventeen, just beginning life, just starting to be noticed, to be admired for not accepting the first proposal she receives? No—pray allow her time to consider her options.”

“I have always considered it a foolish attachment,” Mr. Knightley remarked after a moment, “though I have kept my thoughts to myself; but I now see it will be a regrettable one for Harriet. You will inflate her with notions of her own beauty and of what she is entitled to, until in a short time no one within her reach will seem good enough for her. Pride, when it takes hold of a weak mind, brings about all sorts of trouble. It is so easy for a young lady to expect too much. Miss Harriet Smith may not find proposals of marriage coming in so quickly, though she is a very pretty girl. Men of sense, whatever you may choose to say, do not seek foolish wives. Men of standing would not be particularly eager to link themselves with a girl of such uncertain background—and the most prudent men would be wary of the inconvenience and disgrace they might face when the mystery of her parentage is uncovered. Let her marry Robert Martin, and she is safe, respected, and happy for ever; but if you encourage her to hope for a grander match, and teach her to accept nothing less than a man of importance and considerable fortune, she may end up as a parlour-boarder at Mrs. Goddard’s for the rest of her life—or, at the very least, (for Harriet Smith is a girl who will marry someone or other,) until she becomes desperate and is glad to accept the son of the old writing-master.”

“You and I differ so greatly on this matter, Mr. Knightley, that there is no point in arguing. We shall only make each other more vexed. But as for my _allowing_ her to marry Robert Martin, it is impossible; she has refused him, and so firmly, I think, as must prevent any further attempt. She must suffer the consequences of having refused him, whatever they may be; and as for the refusal itself, I will not pretend to say that I might not have had some influence; but I assure you there was very little for me or anyone else to do. His appearance is so much against him, and his manner so poor, that if she ever were inclined to favor him, she is not now. I can imagine that before she had met anyone better, she might have tolerated him. He was the brother of her friends, and he made an effort to please her; and altogether, having seen nobody more refined (that must have been his great advantage) she might not, while she was at Abbey-Mill, have found him disagreeable. But the situation is different now. She knows what gentlemen are; and nothing but a gentleman in education and manner has any chance with Harriet.”

“Fiddlesticks, absurd fiddlesticks, as ever was said!” exclaimed Mr. Knightley.—“Robert Martin’s manner has sense, sincerity, and good humour to recommend it; and his mind has more true gentility than Harriet Smith could understand.”

Emma said nothing, and tried to appear cheerful and unconcerned, but was truly feeling uneasy and wished him very much to leave.

And he's a really smart kid. They're all incredibly clever, and they have such cute ways. They come and stand by my chair and say, 'Grandpa, can you give me a bit of string?' Once, Henry asked me for a knife, but I told him knives are only for grandpas. I think their dad is too rough with them a lot of the time."

"He seems rough to you," Emma said, "because you're so gentle yourself. But if you compared him with other dads, you wouldn't think he's rough. He wants his boys to be active and tough, and if they misbehave, he can give them a sharp word now and then. But he's a loving father—definitely Mr. John Knightley is a loving father. The kids all like him."

"And then their uncle picks them up and tosses them up to the ceiling in a really scary way!"

"But they love it, Dad. There's nothing they like more. It's such fun for them that if their uncle didn't insist on taking turns, whoever started would never let go."

"Well, I just can't get it."

"That's the case with all of us, Dad. One half of the world can't understand the pleasures of the other."

Later that morning, just as the girls were about to split up before the regular four o'clock dinner, the hero of this unforgettable charade walked in again. Harriet turned away, but Emma could greet him with her usual smile, and her sharp eye quickly noticed that he was aware he had taken a gamble—like rolling the dice—and she thought he was there to see how it would turn out. His stated reason, however, was to ask whether Mr. Woodhouse's group could manage without him in the evening or whether he would be needed at Hartfield. If he was, everything else would have to take a back seat; but if not, his friend Cole had been pushing so much for him to have dinner with him—had made such a big deal about it—that he had promised him conditionally to come.

Emma thanked him, but wouldn't let him disappoint his friend for their sake; her father was definitely getting his usual card game. He pushed again—she refused again; and he seemed about to say goodbye, when she handed him the paper from the table.

He talked like someone really eager to dance; and Emma was a bit surprised to see how clearly the Weston family’s energy was winning out over the more reserved Churchill style. He seemed to have all the liveliness, good mood, and sociable nature of his father, and none of the haughtiness or aloofness that came from Enscombe. In fact, there might not have been enough pride at all; his lack of concern for social status came off as a bit too casual. But he couldn’t really understand the problem with that. It was just a sign of his lively personality.

Eventually, he was convinced to move away from the front of the Crown; and now that they were almost passing the house where the Bates family lived, Emma remembered his planned visit the day before and asked him if he had gone through with it.

“Yes, oh yes!” he replied. “I was just about to mention it. It was a pretty successful visit—I met all three of them, and I’m really grateful for your heads-up. If that talkative aunt had caught me by surprise, it would have been the end of me. As it was, I ended up staying way too long. Ten minutes would have been enough, maybe even more than enough. I had told my dad I’d be home before him—but there was no way out, no chance to pause. And to my complete shock, when he finally found me there, I realized I had been sitting with them for almost forty-five minutes. That nice lady never gave me a chance to leave before that.”

“And what did you think of Miss Fairfax?”

“Ill, really ill—that is, if a young woman can ever be allowed to look unwell. But the term is a bit out of place, Mrs. Weston, isn’t it? Ladies can’t really look ill. And honestly, Miss Fairfax is naturally so pale that she often looks unwell. It’s a real shame she doesn’t have a better complexion.”

Emma didn’t agree and started a passionate defense of Miss Fairfax’s skin. “It’s never been very bright, but I don’t think it usually looks sickly; and there’s a softness and delicacy to her skin that gives her face a special elegance.” He listened politely; admitted he had heard others say the same—but still, he had to admit that he couldn’t imagine anything making up for the lack of a healthy glow. When someone’s features were average, a good complexion could make them look beautiful. And when they were already good, the effect was—luckily, he didn’t need to try to describe what that effect was.

“Well,” said Emma, “there’s no arguing about taste—at least you find her attractive, even if not for her skin.”

He shook his head and laughed. “I can’t really separate Miss Fairfax from her complexion.”

“Did you see her often in Weymouth? Were you often in the same company?”

At that moment, they were approaching Ford’s shop, and he quickly exclaimed, “Hey, this must be the exact shop everyone goes to every day, as my father told me. He says he comes to Highbury himself six days a week and always has business at Ford’s.”

And just yesterday I was telling Mr. Cole that I was really ashamed to look at our new grand piano in the drawing-room, since I can't tell one note from another. Our little girls are just starting out and might never get very good at it. And then there's poor Jane Fairfax, who is very skilled in music, but doesn't have an instrument at all—not even the smallest old harpsichord in the world to play with. I was saying this to Mr. Cole just yesterday, and he agreed with me. He loves music so much that he couldn't help buying the piano, hoping some of our kind neighbors might occasionally use it better than we can. That's really why the instrument was bought—or else I'm sure we should be ashamed of it. We're hoping very much that Miss Woodhouse might try it this evening.”

Miss Woodhouse gave the proper response; and when she saw there was nothing more to be learned from Mrs. Cole, she turned to Frank Churchill.

"Why do you smile?" she asked.

"Nay, why do you?"

"Me!—I suppose I smile because Colonel Campbell is so rich and generous. It's a generous gift."

"Very."

"I wonder why it wasn't given before."

"Perhaps Miss Fairfax has never stayed here this long before."

"Or that he didn't give her the use of their own instrument—which is now locked up in London, untouched by anyone."

"That is a grand piano, and he might think it too big for Mrs. Bates's house."

"You may say what you like—but your expression shows your thoughts on this matter are much like mine."

"I don't know. I think you're giving me more credit for being sharp than I deserve. I smile because you smile, and I'll probably suspect whatever you suspect; but at the moment I don't see what there is to question. If Colonel Campbell isn't the one, who can it be?"

"What about Mrs. Dixon?"

"Mrs. Dixon! That's true enough. I hadn't thought of her. She must know as well as her father how much an instrument would be appreciated; and perhaps the way it was done, the secrecy, the surprise, is more like a young woman's plan than an old man's. It must be Mrs. Dixon, I'm sure. I told you your suspicions would guide mine."

"If so, you must extend your suspicions and include Mr. Dixon as well."

"Mr. Dixon.—Very well. Yes, I see at once that it must be the joint gift of Mr. and Mrs. Dixon. We were talking the other day, you know, about his being such a warm admirer of her playing."

"Yes, and what you told me then confirmed an idea I had before.—I don't mean to question the good intentions of either Mr. Dixon or Miss Fairfax, but I can't help suspecting that, after making his proposals to her friend, he had the misfortune to fall in love with her, or that he became aware of a little affection on her side.

I understand your situation, Miss Woodhouse—(looking toward Mr. Woodhouse)—your father’s health must be a big concern. Why doesn’t he try Bath? He really should. Let me recommend Bath to you. I can assure you I’m convinced it would help Mr. Woodhouse.

“My father tried it more than once before, but it didn’t help at all. And Mr. Perry, whose name I’m sure you know, doesn’t think it would be any more useful now.”

“Ah! That’s a shame. Because I can assure you, Miss Woodhouse, when the waters agree with someone, the relief they give is amazing. I’ve seen so many cases of that in Bath! And it’s such a cheerful place that it couldn’t fail to help Mr. Woodhouse’s spirits, which I understand are sometimes quite low. As for its benefits to you, I don’t need to go on about them. The advantages of Bath for young people are pretty well known. It would be a great experience for you, who’ve lived such a quiet life; and I could immediately connect you with some of the best people there. A note from me would bring you a whole circle of friends; and my special friend, Mrs. Partridge, the woman I’ve always stayed with when I’m in Bath, would be delighted to show you any attention and would be the perfect person for you to go out with in public.”

It was all Emma could do not to be rude. The idea of her being introduced by Mrs. Elton—of her going out in public under the care of a friend of Mrs. Elton’s—probably some vulgar, flashy widow who barely managed to live on her own with the help of a boarder! The dignity of Miss Woodhouse, of Hartfield, was really hurt!

She held herself back from giving any of the reproofs she could have, and only thanked Mrs. Elton coolly; “but going to Bath is completely out of the question; and she wasn’t entirely convinced that the place might suit her better than her father.” And then, to stop any more offense and anger, she changed the subject right away.

“I don’t need to ask whether you’re musical, Mrs. Elton. On these kinds of occasions, a lady’s reputation usually goes ahead of her; and Highbury has long known that you’re a top-class performer.”

old_rewritten_text:
The depth of your admiration might surprise you one day or another.

Mr. Knightley was focused on fastening the lower buttons of his heavy leather gaiters, and either the effort of getting them done or something else brought color to his face as he replied,

“Oh! are you there?—But you’re way behind the times. Mr. Cole gave me a hint about it six weeks ago.”

He paused. Emma felt her foot touched by Mrs. Weston and wasn’t sure what to make of it. A moment later, he continued,

“That will never happen, though. I can assure you. Miss Fairfax, I suppose, wouldn’t have me if I asked—and I’m certain I’ll never ask her.”

Emma returned her friend’s touch with warmth and couldn’t help but say,

“You’re not full of yourself, Mr. Knightley. I’ll give you that much.”

He barely seemed to hear her; he was deep in thought—and soon after, in a tone that showed he wasn’t happy, he said,

“So you’ve been deciding that I should marry Jane Fairfax?”

“No, indeed I haven’t. You’ve been too hard on me for matchmaking for me to go that far with you. What I said just now meant nothing. People say things like that automatically, without any serious intent. Oh no, honestly, I don’t have the slightest desire for you to marry Jane Fairfax or any other Jane. You wouldn’t be sitting with us so comfortably if you were married.”

Mr. Knightley fell into thought again. After a while, he said, “No, Emma, I don’t think the depth of my admiration for her will ever surprise me. I’ve never had any such feelings for her, I assure you.” And shortly after, “Jane Fairfax is a very charming young woman—but not even Jane Fairfax is perfect. She has a flaw. She doesn’t have the open, easygoing nature a man would want in a wife.”

Emma couldn’t help but be glad to hear that she had a flaw. “Well,” she said, “and you shut Mr. Cole up quickly, I suppose?”

“Yes, very quickly. He gave me a quiet hint; I told him he was wrong; he apologized and said no more. Cole doesn’t want to be smarter or cleverer than his neighbors.”

“In that respect, how different from dear Mrs. Elton, who wants to be smarter and cleverer than everyone else! I wonder how she talks about the Coles—what names she gives them! How can she find a name for them that’s vulgar enough? She calls you Knightley—what can she do for Mr. Cole? And so I’m not surprised at all that Jane Fairfax accepts her kindness and agrees to be with her. Mrs. Weston, your point carries the most weight with me. I can much more easily understand the temptation of getting away from Miss Bates than I can believe that Miss Fairfax’s mind would triumph over Mrs. Elton. I don’t believe for a second that Mrs. Elton would ever admit she’s the inferior in thought, word, or deed; or that she’d be held back by anything more than her own limited sense of good manners. I can’t imagine that she won’t keep insulting her guest with praise, encouragement, and offers of help; that she won’t keep talking about her grand plans, from getting her a permanent job to including her in those delightful sightseeing trips in the barouche-landau.”

Woodhouse, I wish you had heard the gallant things he said to me at dinner. Oh! I can assure you I began to think my dear husband would be quite jealous. I imagine I am rather favored; he noticed my gown. What do you think of it?—chosen by Selina—handsome, I believe, though I am uncertain if it is too much adorned; I have a strong aversion to the idea of being overdone—truly dislike extravagance in dress. He stayed at the home of a sluice-keeper on the marshes, and on workdays he would trudge out from his retreat, hands in his pockets, with his lunch loosely wrapped and hanging from his neck. On Sundays, he would mostly lie on the sluice-gates or stand leaning against stacks of hay or barns. He always walked with a slouched gait, as if moving like a locomotive, eyes fixed on the ground; and when he was addressed or otherwise forced to lift them, he would glance up with a mix of irritation and confusion, as if the only thought he ever had was that it was strange and unfair that he never seemed to be thinking.

This sullen journeyman had no fondness for me. When I was small and timid, he let me know that the Devil resided in a dark corner of the forge and that he was well acquainted with the demon. He also claimed it was necessary to build the fire once every seven years using a live boy, and that I should consider myself as potential fuel. When I became Joe’s apprentice, Orlick may have grown more convinced that I would take his place, yet he still disliked me even more. Not that he ever openly showed hostility; I only noticed that he always directed his sparks toward me, and whenever I sang Old Clem, he would interrupt the song unexpectedly.

Dolge Orlick was at the forge the next day when I reminded Joe about my half-holiday. He said nothing at first, for he and Joe had just taken a piece of hot iron between them, and I was tending the bellows; but later, he leaned on his hammer and said:

“Now, master! Surely you’re not going to favor only one of us. If Young Pip has a half-holiday, do as much for Old Orlick.” I suppose he was about twenty-five, but he usually referred to himself as an old man.

“Why, what’ll you do with a half-holiday, if you get it?” said Joe.

“What’ll _I_ do with it! What’ll _he_ do with it? I’ll do as much with it as _him_,” said Orlick.

“As for Pip, he’s going up town,” said Joe.

“Well then, as for Old Orlick, _he_’s a-going up town,” replied the worthy man. “Two can go up town. Tain’t only one wot can go up town.

“Don’t lose your temper,” said Joe.

“Shall if I like,” growled Orlick. “Some and their uptowning! Now, master! Come. No favoring in this shop. Be a man!”

The master refused to consider the matter until the journeyman was in a better mood, so Orlick lunged at the furnace, pulled out a red-hot bar, brandished it at me as if he meant to stab me, swung it around my head, laid it on the anvil, hammered it out—as if it were me, I thought, and the sparks were my flying blood—and finally said, when he had hammered himself hot and the iron cold, and he again leaned on his hammer,

“Now, master!”

“Are you all right now?” demanded Joe.

“Ah! I am all right,” said gruff Old Orlick.

“Then, as in general you stick to your work as well as most men,” said Joe, “let it be a half-holiday for all.”

My sister had been standing quietly in the yard, within earshot—she was a most unscrupulous spy and listener—and she instantly looked in at one of the windows.

Good. You’d better try him in his own house. I’ll make sure the way is clear for you, and you can meet his son first, who’s in London. When are you coming to London?"

"I said (glancing at Joe, who was standing there, motionless and watching), that I thought I could come right away."

"First," said Mr. Jaggers, "you’ll need some new clothes to wear, and they shouldn’t be work clothes. Say next week. You’ll need some money. Should I leave you twenty guineas?"

He pulled out a long purse, completely cool about it, and counted the money out on the table before sliding it toward me. This was the first time he had taken his leg off the chair. He sat straddling the chair after pushing the money over, swinging his purse and watching Joe.

"Well, Joseph Gargery? You look stunned."

"I am!" said Joe, clearly and firmly.

"You remember it was understood that you didn’t want anything for yourself?"

"It was understood," said Joe. "And it still is. And it always will be the same."

"But what," said Mr. Jaggers, swinging his purse, "if it was part of my instructions to give you a gift, as compensation?"

"As compensation for what?" Joe asked.

"For the loss of his services."

Joe put his hand on my shoulder with the tenderness of a woman. I’ve often thought of Joe since, like a steam hammer that could crush a man or gently pat an eggshell, in the way he combined strength with kindness. "Pip is more than welcome," said Joe, "to go free with his services, to honor and fortune, more than words can say. But if you think money can make up for the loss of the little boy who came to the forge—and the best of friends—"

Oh, dear good Joe, whom I was so ready to leave and so ungrateful to, I see you again, with your strong blacksmith’s arm in front of your eyes, your broad chest heaving, and your voice fading away. Oh, dear good, faithful, tender Joe, I feel the loving tremble of your hand on my arm, as solemnly today as if it had been the rustle of an angel’s wing.

But I reassured Joe at the time. I was lost in the excitement of my future fortune and couldn’t go back over the little paths we had walked together. I asked Joe to be comforted, for (as he said) we had always been the best of friends, and (as I said) we always would be. Joe rubbed his eyes with his free wrist, as if he were trying to gouge them out, but said nothing else.

Mr. Jaggers had watched this, as if he saw Joe as the village idiot and me as his keeper. When it was over, he said, holding the purse in his hand after he had stopped swinging it:

"Now, Joseph Gargery, I warn you this is your last chance. No half measures with me. If you want to accept a gift that I’m here to give you, speak up, and you’ll get it. If, on the other hand, you mean to say—" Here, to his great surprise, he was cut off by Joe suddenly turning on him with every sign of a fierce pugilistic intent.

And yet I can't," said Mr. Pumblechook, standing up again, "see one person—and also raise a glass to one person—without once more saying—Can I—can I really—?"
  
  "Sure," I said, and he shook my hand again, finished his glass, and turned it upside down. I did the same; and if I had flipped myself upside down before drinking, the wine couldn't have gone to my head any faster.
  
  Mr. Pumblechook helped me get the liver portion and the best slice of tongue (no more obscure No Thoroughfares of Pork now), and he hardly took care of himself at all. "Ah! Poultry, poultry! You never imagined," said Mr. Pumblechook, addressing the bird on the plate, "when you were a little chick what was in store for you. You never imagined you'd be a treat under this humble roof for someone who—Call it a weakness if you like," said Mr. Pumblechook, standing up again, "but can I—can I really—?"
  
  It was getting to the point where it wasn't necessary to keep saying I could, so he just did it. How he managed to do it so often without cutting himself with my knife, I don't know.
  
  "And your sister," he continued after a few bites, "who had the honor of raising you by hand! It's a sad thought, to realize she's no longer capable of fully understanding the honor. Can—"
  
  I saw he was about to go at me again, so I stopped him.
  
  "Let's drink to her health," I said.
  
  "Ah!" cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, completely relaxed with admiration, "that's how you recognize them, sir!" (I don't know who Sir was, but it certainly wasn't me, and there was no one else there); "that's how you recognize the noble-minded, sir! Always forgiving and always approachable. It might," said the fawning Pumblechook, setting down his untouched glass in a rush and standing up again, "to a regular person, look like repeating—but can I—can I really—?"
  
  After he did it, he sat back down and raised a toast to my sister. "Let us never forget," said Mr. Pumblechook, "her temperamental flaws, but it's to be hoped she meant well."
  
  Around this time, I started to notice that his face was getting flushed; as for myself, I felt my whole face, soaked in wine and burning.
  
  I told Mr. Pumblechook that I wanted my new clothes sent to his house, and he was thrilled that I trusted him so much. I explained why I wanted to avoid being noticed in the village, and he praised me to the skies. He hinted that no one else was worthy of my trust, and—well, could he? Then he asked me gently if I remembered our childhood math games and how we had gone together to have me become his apprentice, and essentially, how he had always been my favorite imaginary friend and my chosen buddy? If I had had ten times as many glasses of wine as I had, I would have known that he had never been in that position with me, and I would have rejected the idea deep in my heart. Yet, despite that, I remember feeling convinced that I had been wrong about him, and that he was a sensible, practical, good-hearted guy.

I then realized that Wemmick was the clerk in the next office. Another clerk was called down from upstairs to take his place while he was away, and I walked out with him after shaking hands with my guardian. We found a group of new people hanging around outside, but Wemmick pushed through them by saying coolly but firmly, 'I'm telling you, it's no good; he won't say a word to any of you.' We quickly got past them and walked side by side down the street.

Chapter XXI.

Looking at Mr. Wemmick as we walked, trying to get a better sense of him in the daylight, I saw that he was a dry, somewhat short man with a square, wooden face. His expression looked like it had been roughly carved out with a dull chisel. There were a few marks that might have been dimples if the material had been softer and the tool sharper, but as it was, they were just dents. The chisel had tried three or four times to add some decoration over his nose, but had given up without bothering to smooth it out. I figured he was single from the worn-out state of his clothes, and he seemed to have gone through a lot of losses; he wore at least four mourning rings, plus a brooch showing a lady and a weeping willow next to a tomb with an urn on it. I also noticed that several rings and seals hung from his watch chain, as if he was weighed down with memories of people who had passed away. His eyes were bright—small, sharp, and black—and his lips were thin, wide, and mottled. I guessed he was somewhere between forty and fifty years old.

'So you've never been to London before?' Mr. Wemmick asked me.

'No,' I said.

'I was new here once,' Mr. Wemmick replied. 'Funny to think about now!'

'You know the city well now?'

'Well, yeah,' said Mr. Wemmick. 'I know how it works.'

'Is it a really bad place?' I asked, more to say something than anything else.

'You can get cheated, robbed, or even killed in London. But there are plenty of people anywhere who'll do that for you.'

'If there's bad blood between you and them,' I added, trying to soften it a bit.

'Oh, I don't know about bad blood,' Mr. Wemmick replied. 'There's not much bad blood around. They'll do it if there's something in it for them.'

'That makes it worse.'

'You think so?' Mr. Wemmick said. 'I'd say it's pretty much the same either way.'

He wore his hat tilted to the back of his head and looked straight ahead, walking in a self-contained way as if nothing in the streets could catch his attention. His mouth had such a mechanical, post-office-like quality that it gave him the appearance of smiling. Don’t waste your time on pointless efforts. Why would you? Now, who’s next?”

So we strolled through Wemmick’s greenhouse until he stopped and said, “Watch the man I’m about to shake hands with.” I would have noticed him anyway since he hadn’t shaken hands with anyone yet.

Almost as soon as he said that, a tall, broad-shouldered man (whom I can still picture clearly now) in a well-worn olive-colored coat, with a strange grayish tint to his red complexion and eyes that darted around when he tried to focus, approached a corner of the bars and touched his hat—which had a greasy, cold-broth-like surface—with a half-serious, half-joking military salute.

“Colonel, to you!” Wemmick said. “How are you, Colonel?”

“All right, Mr. Wemmick.”

“We did everything we could, but the evidence was too strong against us, Colonel.”

“Yes, it was too strong, sir—but I don’t care.”

“No, no,” Wemmick said coolly. “You don’t care.” Then, turning to me, “This guy served His Majesty. He was a regular soldier and bought his discharge.”

I said, “Indeed?” and the man’s eyes looked at me, then over my head, then all around me, and then he ran his hand across his lips and laughed.

“I think I’ll be out of here on Monday, sir,” he said to Wemmick.

“Maybe,” my friend replied. “But who knows?”

“I’m glad to have the chance to say goodbye to you, Mr. Wemmick,” the man said, holding out his hand between two bars.

“Thanks,” Wemmick said, shaking his hand. “Same to you, Colonel.”

“If what I had on me when I was caught had been real, Mr. Wemmick,” the man said, not wanting to let go of his hand, “I’d have asked you to wear another ring—as a token of your kindness.”

“I’ll take the sentiment as the action,” Wemmick said. “By the way; you were quite a pigeon fancier.” The man looked up at the sky. “I’m told you had a remarkable line of tumblers. Could you ask a friend to bring me a pair, if you don’t need them anymore?”

“It’ll be done, sir.”

“All right,” Wemmick said. “They’ll be taken care of. Good afternoon, Colonel. Good-bye!” They shook hands again, and as we walked away, Wemmick said to me, “A forger, a very good craftsman. The Recorder’s report is in today, and he’s definitely going to be hanged on Monday. Still, you see, as far as it goes, a pair of pigeons are still portable property.” With that, he looked back and nodded at the dead plant, then glanced around as he walked out of the yard, as if considering which other pot would fit best in its place.

As we left the prison through the lodge, I noticed that the turnkeys valued my guardian just as much as the people they held. “Well, Mr. Wemmick,” said the turnkey who kept us between the two studded and spiked lodge gates, carefully locking one before unlocking the other, “what’s Mr. Jaggers going to do about that water-side murder?”

When evaluating an author's worth and determining their place among the literary pantheon, we are justified in assessing them from our own perspective and according to our own criteria. Yet, when considering the strength of their work, we must take into account their original intent and compare their creations to the vision they themselves set forth, measuring how much falls short. We differ from Mr. Poe in our views on the aims of art. He believes the goal is the creation of Beauty, and it may be only in the interpretation of that term that we find ourselves at odds. In our remarks on his writings, however, we shall follow his own standard as our guide. The sanctuary of the muse is open from every direction, and there is ample space within it for all who offer tribute or seek prophecy.

In his stories, Mr. Poe has chosen to demonstrate his talent primarily in that shadowy realm that lies at the edge of the plausible and stretches into the strange boundaries of superstition and the unreal. He possesses a striking ability to blend two faculties rarely found together: the capacity to affect the reader's mind with the subtle suggestions of mystery and an attention to detail so thorough that not even a pin or a button escapes notice. Both traits stem naturally from the dominant feature of his intellect, which we have previously mentioned—analysis. This is what sets the artist apart. His mind immediately grasps the desired effect. Once he has decided to evoke certain feelings in the reader, he ensures that every element contributes precisely to the central aim. Even his mystery is calculated in his mind. To him, X is a known variable throughout. In any scene he creates, he understands the chemical nature of all his colors. Although some of his figures may appear indistinct, and the shadows formless, to him the contours are as clear and defined as those of a geometric figure. For this reason, Mr. Poe has no affinity for Mysticism. The Mystic lives within the mystery, is wrapped in it; it tinges all his thoughts; it especially affects his vision, and the most ordinary things acquire a prismatic glow from it. Mr. Poe, by contrast, is an observer from the outside. He examines, he dissects, he watches

“with an eye serene,
The very pulse of the machine,”

for it is essentially a machine to him, with gears and cogs and piston-rods, all working to achieve a specific outcome.

This analytical nature of his mind tempers the poetic, and by giving him the endurance to be meticulous, allows him to inject a remarkable sense of reality into his most fantastical ideas. A monomania he portrays with great strength. He enjoys dissecting one of these mental tumors and tracing all the delicate extensions of its roots. In conjuring images of horror, too, he achieves unusual success, sometimes conveying to us by a faint suggestion some dreadful uncertainty, which is the essence of all horror. He leaves the imagination the task of completing the picture, a task to which only it is suited.

“For much imaginary work was there;
Conceit deceitful, so compact, so kind,
That for Achilles’ image stood his spear
Grasped in an armed hand; himself behind
Was left unseen, save to the eye of mind.”

In about four and a half hours, I found the balloon sufficiently inflated. I attached the car and placed all my tools inside, including the condensing apparatus, plenty of water, and a large amount of food like pemmican, which is very nutritious but takes up little space. I also put a pair of pigeons and a cat in the car. It was almost morning, and I thought it was time to leave. I dropped a lit cigar on the ground as if by accident, and while I bent down to pick it up, I quietly lit the fuse that extended slightly from the bottom of one of the smaller barrels. The three men didn't notice this at all. I jumped into the car, cut the single rope that tied me to the ground, and was happy to see that I rose easily, carrying 175 pounds of lead ballast, and could have carried just as much more.

"However, I had barely reached a height of fifty yards when a terrible storm of fire, smoke, sulfur, legs, arms, gravel, burning wood, and flaming metal came roaring up after me in the most frightening and chaotic way. My heart sank, and I fell to the bottom of the car, shaking with pure fear. I realized then that I had gone too far, and the worst effects of the explosion were yet to come. In less than a second, I felt all the blood rush to my temples, and then a shock, which I will never forget, burst through the night and seemed to tear the sky apart. Later, when I had time to think, I didn't fail to blame the extreme force of the explosion on my position directly above it and in the path of its greatest power. But at the time, I only thought of saving my life. The balloon first collapsed, then violently expanded, then spun around with terrifying speed, and finally, swaying and staggering like a drunk man, it threw me with great force over the edge of the car and left me hanging, at a terrifying height, with my head down and my face outward, by a thin piece of cord about three feet long, which hung accidentally through a crack near the bottom of the wicker, and in which, as I fell, my left foot became very conveniently entangled. It is impossible to imagine the horror of my situation. I gasped for breath, a shudder like a fit of the ague shook every nerve and muscle in my body, I felt my eyes popping from their sockets, a terrible nausea overwhelmed me, and finally I fainted.

"How long I remained in this state is impossible to say. It must, however, have been some time, for when I partially regained my senses, I found the day breaking, the balloon at a great height over an endless ocean, and not a trace of land to be seen far and wide within the vast horizon.

Upon arriving at the hut, I knocked as was my habit, and receiving no answer, I searched for the key in the spot I knew it was hidden, unlocked the door, and stepped inside. A pleasant fire was burning in the fireplace. It was a welcome sight, and I was glad to see it. I removed my coat, took a chair by the crackling logs, and waited calmly for my hosts to arrive.

Soon after nightfall they came, greeting me with great warmth. Jupiter, beaming with delight, bustled around preparing some marsh hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his fits—how else can I describe them?—of excitement. He had discovered an unfamiliar bivalve, which he believed formed a new genus, and more than that, he had tracked down and captured, with Jupiter’s help, a _scarabæus_ that he thought might be entirely new, though he wanted my opinion on the matter the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, rubbing my hands by the fire, wishing the whole tribe of _scarabæi_ were far away.

“Ah, if only I had known you were here!” Legrand replied. “It’s been so long since I last saw you, and how could I have imagined you would visit on this very night of all nights? On my way home I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and, foolishly, I lent him the bug. So you won’t be able to see it until morning. Stay here tonight, and I’ll send Jup to fetch it at sunrise. It is the most beautiful thing in existence!”

“What?—sunrise?”

“Nonsense! No!—the bug. It is a brilliant gold color—about the size of a large hickory-nut—with two jet black spots near one end of the back, and another, a bit longer, at the other. The _antennæ_ are—”

“Dey ain’t no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep a tellin on you,” Jupiter interjected. “De bug is a goole bug, solid, ebery bit of him, inside and all, sep him wing—neber feel half so hebby a bug in my life.”

“Well, suppose it is, Jup,” Legrand replied, with more urgency than the situation seemed to require, “is that any reason for you to let the birds burn? The color”—he turned to me—“is really almost enough to support Jupiter’s idea. You have never seen a more brilliant metallic sheen than the scales emit—but you cannot judge that until tomorrow. In the meantime, I can give you some idea of the shape.” With that, he sat down at a small table where a pen and ink were placed, but there was no paper. He searched a drawer for some, but found none.

“Never mind,” he said at last, “this will do.” And from his waistcoat pocket he pulled out a scrap of what I assumed to be very dirty foolscap, and sketched a rough drawing with the pen. While he did this, I remained seated by the fire, still feeling the chill. When the sketch was finished, he handed it to me without getting up. As I took it, a loud growl was heard, followed by scratching at the door. Jupiter opened it, and a large Newfoundland belonging to Legrand came in, leaping onto my shoulders and showering me with affection; for I had shown him much attention during my previous visits.

old_rewritten_text:
I feared that the unrelenting weight of misfortune had finally driven my friend to the edge of reason. Without a moment's delay, I decided to accompany the negro.

When we arrived at the dock, I observed a scythe and three spades, all brand new, resting at the bottom of the boat we were to use.

“What is the purpose of these, Jup?” I asked.

“Him syfe, massa, and spade.”

“Indeed; but why are they here?”

“Him de syfe and de spade what Massa Will told me to buy for him in town, and it cost me a fortune to get ’em.”

“But what, in the name of all that is strange, is your ‘Massa Will’ going to do with scythes and spades?”

“That’s more than I know, and the devil take me if I don’t think it’s more than he knows too. But it’s all because of that bug.”

Since I could gain no clarity from Jupiter, whose mind seemed entirely consumed by 'de bug,' I stepped into the boat and we set sail. With a brisk wind at our backs, we quickly reached the small cove north of Fort Moultrie, and a two-mile walk brought us to the hut. It was about three in the afternoon when we arrived. Legrand had been waiting for us with great anticipation. He seized my hand with a nervous eagerness that unsettled me and reinforced my suspicions. His face was pale, almost deathly so, and his deep-set eyes gleamed with an unnatural brightness. After a few inquiries about his health, I asked him, not knowing what else to say, if he had yet obtained the _scarabæus_ from Lieutenant G——.

“Oh, yes,” he replied, his face flushing, “I got it from him the next morning. Nothing would tempt me to part with that _scarabæus_. Do you know that Jupiter is quite right about it?”

“In what way?” I asked, with a growing sense of unease.

“In thinking it is a bug made of _real gold_.” He spoke with such solemnity that I felt a deep sense of shock.

“This bug is going to make my fortune,” he continued, with a triumphant grin, “to restore me to my family’s estate. Is it any wonder, then, that I value it? Since Fortune has seen fit to give it to me, I only need to use it properly and I shall find the gold it points to. Jupiter; bring me that _scarabæus!_”

“What! de bug, massa? I’d rather not go fetch that bug for you—you must get him for yourself.” Legrand then rose with a solemn and dignified manner and retrieved the beetle from a glass case where it was kept. It was a beautiful scarabæus, and, at that time, unknown to naturalists—naturally a great treasure from a scientific standpoint. There were two round, black spots near one end of its back, and a long one near the other. The scales were incredibly hard and shiny, with the look of polished gold. The weight of the insect was remarkable, and, considering all these things, I could hardly fault Jupiter for his belief about it; but what to make of Legrand’s agreement with that belief, I could not, for the life of me, understand.

old_rewritten_text:
I’m sorry; I forgot that Shakespeare won’t be around for seventeen hundred and fifty more years. But doesn’t the city of Epidaphne support my claim that it looks strange?

'It is well protected; and in this way, it owes as much to nature as to human effort.'

That's true.

'There are many grand palaces.'

There are.

'And the many temples, which are rich and impressive, can compare with the best of ancient times.'

I agree with all that. Still, there are also countless shabby huts and terrible hovels. We can't help but notice the filth in every gutter, and if it weren’t for the strong smell of incense from the idols, I’m sure we’d find a terrible stench. Have you ever seen streets so unbearably narrow, or houses so incredibly tall? What darkness their shadows cast on the ground! It’s good that the hanging lamps in those endless colonnades are lit all day; otherwise, we would have the darkness of Egypt during its worst times.

'It is certainly a strange place! What is that unusual building over there? Look! It rises above all the others and lies to the east of what I think is the royal palace!'

That is the new Temple of the Sun, which is worshipped in Syria under the name Elah Gabalah. In the future, a very famous Roman emperor will start this worship in Rome and get his nickname from it, Heliogabalus. I bet you would like to see the god of the temple. You don’t need to look up at the sky; his Sunship isn’t there—at least not the one the Syrians worship. That god can be found inside that building. He is worshipped as a large stone pillar that ends in a cone or pyramid, which represents Fire.

'Listen—look!—who are those silly people, half naked, with their faces painted, shouting and gesturing to the crowd?'

Some are just performers. Others are more like philosophers. Most of them, especially those who hit the crowd with sticks, are the main courtiers of the palace, doing their duty to carry out some amusing act ordered by the king.

'But what do we have here? Goodness! The town is full of wild animals! What a terrible sight!—what a dangerous feature!'

Terrible, if you want to call it that; but not at all dangerous. Each animal, if you take the time to notice, is quietly following its master. A few are led by a rope around the neck, but these are mostly the smaller or timid kinds. The lion, the tiger, and the leopard are completely free. They have been trained easily for their current jobs and follow their owners like personal attendants. It is true, there are times when Nature reclaims what has been taken from her;—but then the eating of a soldier, or the choking of a sacred bull, is a small matter and not worth mentioning in Epidaphne.

'But what strange noise do I hear? Surely this is a loud noise even for Antioch! It suggests some unusual excitement.'

“There’s still no clue at all to this terrible mystery,” we believe.

The next day’s paper had more details.

“The Tragedy in the Rue Morgue.—Many people have been questioned about this strange and horrifying incident,” [The word ‘affaire’ hasn’t yet, in France, taken on the casual meaning it has for us], “but nothing has come to light. We present below all the relevant testimony gathered.

“Pauline Dubourg, a laundress, says she’s known both the deceased for three years, having done their laundry during that time. The older woman and her daughter seemed to get along well—very affectionate with each other. They paid well. She couldn’t say anything about how they lived. She thought Madame L. made a living telling fortunes. She was believed to have saved money. She never met anyone in the house when she dropped off or picked up the laundry. She was sure they didn’t have a servant. There didn’t seem to be any furniture in the building except on the fourth floor.

“Pierre Moreau, a tobacconist, says he’s sold small amounts of tobacco and snuff to Madame L’Espanaye for almost four years. He was born nearby and has always lived there. The deceased and her daughter had lived in the house where the bodies were found for over six years. It was previously occupied by a jeweler, who sublet the upper rooms to different people. The house belonged to Madame L. She became unhappy with how her tenants used the place and moved in herself, refusing to rent out any part. The older woman acted childishly. He had seen the daughter maybe five or six times in the six years. The two lived a very private life—were said to have money. He’d heard neighbors say Madame L. told fortunes—but he didn’t believe it. He’d never seen anyone else enter the house except the old woman and her daughter, a porter once or twice, and a doctor about eight or ten times.

“Many other neighbors gave similar testimony. No one was mentioned as regularly visiting the house. It wasn’t known if Madame L. and her daughter had any living relatives. The shutters on the front windows were rarely open. Those on the back were always closed, except for the large back room on the fourth floor. The house was a decent one—not very old.

“Isidore Musèt, a gendarme, says he was called to the house around three in the morning and found about twenty or thirty people at the gate trying to get in. He forced it open with a bayonet—not a crowbar. It wasn’t hard to open because it was a double or folding gate and wasn’t bolted at the top or bottom. The screams continued until the gate was forced open—and then suddenly stopped. They sounded like someone (or some people) in great pain—long and loud, not short and quick. He led the way upstairs. When he reached the first landing, he heard two voices in loud and angry argument—the one a rough voice, the other much higher—a very strange voice.”

old_rewritten_text:
Knowing what they owed to the child they had brought into the world, and because they both had kind and caring hearts, it's easy to imagine that during every hour of my early life I was taught patience, charity, and self-control. It all felt like a smooth path of happiness to me.

For a long time, I was the only child they had. My mother had always wanted a daughter, but I remained their only child. When I was about five years old, they went on a trip beyond the borders of Italy and spent a week by the shores of Lake Como. Their kind and generous nature often led them to visit the homes of poor people. For my mother, this was more than a duty; it was a need, almost a passion. She remembered her own suffering and how she had been helped, and now she wanted to be like an angel to those in need. During one of their walks, they came across a poor cottage in a valley that looked especially sad. The number of half-clothed children around it showed how poor the family was. One day, when my father had gone alone to Milan, my mother took me to visit this home. She found a hardworking peasant and his wife, worn down by worry and work, giving a meager meal to five hungry children. Among them, one child stood out to my mother more than the rest. She looked different from the others. The other four were dark-eyed and tough little kids; this child was thin and very pale. Her hair was the brightest gold, and even though her clothes were poor, it seemed to crown her head with a special glow. Her forehead was clear and wide, her blue eyes bright and clear, and her lips and face showed such sensitivity and sweetness that no one could look at her without thinking she was a special being, almost sent from heaven.

The peasant woman, noticing that my mother was looking at this lovely girl with wonder and admiration, eagerly told her the girl's story. She wasn't her own child, but the daughter of a nobleman from Milan. Her mother was German and had died giving birth to her. The baby had been left with these people to be raised, and they had been better off back then. They had not been married long, and their oldest child had just been born. The father of the girl was one of those Italians who remembered the ancient glory of their country and tried to win back their freedom. He became a victim of his country's weakness. It wasn't known if he had died or was still in Austrian prisons. His property was taken away, and his child became an orphan and a beggar. She stayed with her foster parents and grew up in their simple home, more beautiful than a garden rose among dark-leaved brambles.

When my father returned from Milan, he found a child playing with me in the hall of our villa who was more beautiful than any painted angel—a child who seemed to shine with light from her looks and who moved more lightly than the mountain goats.

“Fiend,” I cried, “do you dare come near me? Do you not fear the terrible wrath of my hand falling upon your wretched skull? Away, foul creature! Or stay, so that I might crush you beneath my feet! And oh, if only I could end your pitiful life and bring back those you have so cruelly taken away!”

“I foresaw this response,” the demon replied. “All men despise the wretched; how much more must I be despised, being the most wretched of all beings! Yet you, my maker, loathe and reject me, your creation, to whom you are bound by ties that can only be broken by the destruction of one of us. You intend to kill me. How dare you toy with life in this way? Fulfill your duty to me, and I shall fulfill mine to you and to mankind. If you agree to my terms, I shall leave you and your kin in peace; but if you refuse, I shall feed the jaws of death until they are sated with the blood of your remaining loved ones.”

“Accursed wretch! Monster that you are! The torments of hell are too lenient for your sins. Miserable demon! You accuse me of your creation—come then, that I may snuff out the spark I so carelessly gave you.”

My fury knew no bounds; I leapt at him, driven by every feeling that could drive one being to destroy another.

He easily avoided me and said,

“Calm yourself! I beg you to listen to me before you unleash your hatred upon my doomed head. Have I not suffered enough, that you would add to my sorrow? Life, though it may be nothing but a collection of sorrows, is precious to me, and I shall defend it. Remember, you have made me stronger than yourself; my height surpasses yours, my joints more flexible. But I will not be lured into opposing you. I am your creation, and I shall be gentle and obedient to my rightful master and king if you, too, fulfill your part, which you owe me. Oh, Frankenstein, do not be just to all others and trample upon me alone, to whom your justice, and even your mercy and affection, are most deserved. Recall that I am your creation; I should be your Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel, whom you drive from joy for no wrongdoing. Everywhere I see happiness, from which I alone am forever excluded. I was kind and good; misery turned me into a monster. Make me happy, and I shall once more be virtuous.”

“Leave me! I will not listen to you. There can be no bond between you and me; we are enemies. Leave, or let us test our strength in a battle, in which one must fall.”

“How can I stir you? Will no pleas cause you to look upon your creature with kindness, who begs for your goodness and compassion? Believe me, Frankenstein, I was kind; my soul burned with love and humanity; but am I not alone, dreadfully alone? You, my creator, despise me; what hope can I have from your fellow men, who owe me nothing? They reject and hate me. The lonely mountains and bleak glaciers are my sanctuary. I have wandered here for many days; the icy caves, which I do not fear, are my home, and the only one which man does not begrudge.

“How can I stir you? Will no pleas cause you to look upon your creature with kindness, who begs for your goodness and compassion? Believe me, Frankenstein, I was kind; my soul burned with love and humanity; but am I not alone, dreadfully alone? You, my creator, despise me; what hope can I have from your fellow men, who owe me nothing? They reject and hate me. The lonely mountains and bleak glaciers are my sanctuary. I have wandered here for many days; the icy caves, which I do not fear, are my home, and the only one which man does not begrudge.

old_rewritten_text:
The poor who came to their door were never turned away. I admit, I asked for more than just a little food or a place to rest—I wanted kindness and sympathy. I didn’t think I was completely unworthy of it.

The winter had advanced, and a full cycle of the seasons had passed since I came to life. At this point, my focus was entirely on how to introduce myself to the people in the cottage who had helped me. I considered many plans, but the one I finally settled on was to enter the house when the blind old man was alone. I was smart enough to realize that the unnatural ugliness of my appearance was what scared people most when they saw me before. My voice, though rough, wasn’t really frightening, so I thought that if I could win over the old De Lacey while his kids were away, he might help me gain acceptance from the younger ones.

One day, the sun shone on the red leaves scattered on the ground, bringing a bit of cheerfulness even though it didn’t offer much warmth. Safie, Agatha, and Felix went for a long walk in the countryside, and the old man, as he had asked, stayed alone in the cottage. After his kids left, he picked up his guitar and played several sad but sweet tunes, sadder and sweeter than I had ever heard him play before. At first, his face showed pleasure, but as he played on, his expression turned thoughtful and sad. Eventually, he put the instrument aside and sat lost in thought.

My heart raced. This was the moment of truth, the time that would either bring my hopes to life or confirm my fears. The servants had gone to a nearby fair. Everything was quiet in and around the cottage—it was the perfect chance. Yet, when I tried to carry out my plan, my legs gave out and I collapsed to the ground. I got up again, mustering all the strength I could, and removed the planks I had placed in front of my hovel to hide my hiding place. The fresh air revived me, and with renewed determination, I walked toward the door of their cottage.

I knocked. 'Who is it?' the old man asked. 'Come in.'

I stepped inside. 'Sorry to bother you,' I said. 'I'm a traveler in need of a little rest. I'd really appreciate it if you'd let me sit by the fire for a few minutes.'

'Come in,' De Lacey said. 'I'll do what I can to help you out, but unfortunately, my kids are out, and since I'm blind, I'm afraid I'll have a hard time getting you anything to eat.'

'Don't trouble yourself, kind sir,' I replied. 'I've got food. All I need is warmth and a bit of rest.'

I sat down, and a silence followed. I knew every minute was precious, but I still couldn't decide how to start the conversation when the old man finally spoke.

'By your accent, stranger, I'd guess you're from my country. Are you French?'

'No,' I said. 'I was raised by a French family and only speak that language. I'm heading to some friends I truly care about and hope they'll welcome me.'

old_rewritten_text:
I spent the rest of the day in my hovel in complete and hopeless despair. My protectors had left, and they had broken the only connection I had to the world. For the first time, feelings of revenge and hatred filled my heart, and I didn't try to control them. I let myself be carried away by these emotions, focusing my thoughts on harm and death. When I thought of my friends, the kind voice of De Lacey, the gentle eyes of Agatha, and the beauty of the Arabian girl, these thoughts disappeared for a moment, and I cried a bit, which gave me some comfort. But when I remembered that they had rejected and abandoned me, anger returned, a strong and fierce anger. Since I couldn't hurt anyone, I turned my anger toward objects. As night grew, I gathered different flammable materials around the cottage and destroyed all signs of cultivation in the garden. I waited impatiently until the moon had set before I began my plan.

"As the night went on, a strong wind rose from the woods and quickly scattered the clouds that had lingered in the sky. The wind blew like a huge avalanche and made me feel wild and out of control. I lit a dry branch of a tree and danced around the cottage with fury, my eyes fixed on the western horizon where the moon was almost touching. Part of the moon disappeared, and I waved my burning branch. It sank, and with a loud scream, I set fire to the straw, heath, and bushes I had gathered. The wind helped the fire spread, and the cottage was soon surrounded by flames, which clung to it and licked it with their forked and destructive tongues.

"As soon as I was sure that no help could save any part of the house, I left the scene and found shelter in the woods.

"Now, with the world before me, where should I go? I decided to run far from the place of my misfortunes; but to me, hated and despised, every country would be equally terrible. Eventually, the thought of you came to my mind. I learned from your papers that you were my father, my creator; and who else could I turn to but the one who had given me life? Among the lessons that Felix had given Safie, geography had not been left out; I had learned from these the positions of the different countries on the earth. You had mentioned Geneva as the name of your hometown, and toward this place I decided to go.

"But how was I to find my way? I knew I had to travel in a southwesterly direction to reach my destination, but the sun was my only guide. I didn't know the names of the towns I would pass through, nor could I ask for help from anyone. But I didn't give up. Only from you could I hope for help, although I felt nothing but hatred toward you. Unfeeling, heartless creator! You gave me senses and emotions and then left me out in the world to be the object of human scorn and fear.

old_rewritten_text:
The crime started with her—let her face the consequences! Thanks to Felix's teachings and the brutal laws of society, I had learned how to cause trouble. I leaned over her and carefully tucked the portrait into one of the folds of her dress. She moved again, and I ran away.

For a few days, I kept returning to the place where these events happened, sometimes hoping to see you, sometimes determined to leave the world and its pain behind forever. Eventually, I headed toward these mountains and wandered through their vast, empty spaces, driven by a burning passion only you can satisfy. We won't part ways until you promise to meet my demand. I'm alone and miserable; no one wants to be around me. But someone as deformed and terrible as I am wouldn't turn me away. My partner must be from the same species and share my flaws. You're the only one who can create this being for me.'

The creature finished speaking and stared at me, waiting for my response. But I was confused, overwhelmed, and couldn't think clearly enough to grasp the full weight of his request. He went on,

'You must create a female for me, someone I can live with and share the feelings I need to survive. Only you can do this, and I'm demanding it as a right you can't deny me.'

The second part of his story reignited the anger I had forgotten while he described his peaceful life with the cottagers, and when he said this, I could no longer hold back the rage inside me.

'I refuse,' I said. 'No amount of pain will ever make me agree. You can make me the saddest person alive, but you'll never make me feel ashamed. Would you really create another like yourself, whose combined evil could destroy the world? Leave me alone! I've answered you; you can hurt me all you want, but I'll never say yes.'

'You're wrong,' the creature replied. 'Instead of threatening me, I'm willing to talk things out with you. I'm cruel because I'm unhappy. Don't I get shunned and hated by everyone? You, my creator, would tear me apart and feel victorious. Remember that, and tell me why I should care about humans more than they care about me? You wouldn't call it murder if you threw me into one of those ice cracks and ended my life, which you made. Should I respect people who condemn me? Let them live with me in kindness, and I'd give them everything I could with tears of gratitude for accepting me. But that's impossible; human nature is an unbreakable wall between us. Still, I won't accept the submission of a slave. I'll take revenge for my suffering; if I can't inspire love, I'll inspire fear, especially toward you, my worst enemy, because you're my creator. I swear I'll never stop hating you. Be careful; I'll destroy you, and I won't stop until your heart is broken and you curse the day you were born.'

A furious anger showed in his face as he said this; his expression twisted into something too awful to look at. But soon he calmed down and continued,

'I meant to reason.'

old_rewritten_text:
Things had definitely changed for me. My health, which had been getting worse, was now much better, and my mood, when I wasn't weighed down by the memory of my unhappy promise, had lifted right along with it. My father noticed this and was pleased. He started thinking about the best way to get rid of the last traces of my sadness, which would sometimes come back in waves, dark and all-consuming, even when the sun was about to shine again. During those times, I would retreat into complete solitude. I would spend entire days alone on the lake in a small boat, watching the clouds and listening to the gentle lapping of the waves, feeling quiet and unmotivated. But the fresh air and bright sun usually helped me feel calmer, and when I came back, I greeted my friends with a more cheerful smile and a lighter heart.

It was after one of these outings that my father pulled me aside and spoke to me like this:

“I’m glad to see, my dear son, that you’ve started enjoying the things you used to again and seem to be getting back to your old self. And yet, you still seem unhappy and avoid our company. For a while, I wasn’t sure why, but yesterday it hit me. If I’m right, I urge you to tell me. Keeping things to yourself on this issue would not only be pointless, but it would bring even more misery to all of us.”

I shook badly at the start of his speech, and he went on:

“I’ll admit, my son, that I’ve always imagined your marriage to our dear Elizabeth as the foundation of our family’s happiness and the support of my old age. You two have been close since childhood; you studied together and seemed perfectly matched in personality and interests. But human experience is so limited that what I thought would help bring things together might have actually torn it apart. Perhaps you see her as your sister, with no desire for her to become your wife. Or maybe you’ve met someone else you love, and the pressure of feeling honor-bound to Elizabeth is causing the deep pain you seem to be going through.”

“My dear father, don’t worry. I love my cousin deeply and genuinely. I’ve never met a woman who inspires in me the kind of admiration and affection Elizabeth does. My future hopes and dreams are all tied to the idea of us being together.”

“Hearing you speak like this, my dear Victor, brings me more joy than I’ve felt in a while. If you feel that way, we’ll surely be happy, even if current events cast a shadow over us. But it’s this shadow that seems to have taken such a strong hold on your mind that I want to lift. Tell me, then, if you have any objections to getting married right away. We’ve had bad luck, and recent events have disrupted the peace I need for my age and health. You’re younger, but I don’t think, with the fortune you have, that getting married early would interfere with any future plans you might have for honor and usefulness.”

I thought I could land almost anywhere, but I couldn’t—the bank was too steep. I got to the bottom of the island before I found a good spot. I went into the woods and decided I wouldn’t fool around with rafts anymore, as long as they kept moving the lantern around. I had my pipe, some tobacco, and matches in my cap, and they weren’t wet, so I was all set.

“And you haven’t had any meat or bread to eat all this time? Why didn’t you get mud-turtles?”

“How would you catch them? You can’t sneak up on them and grab them, and how would you hit them with a rock? How could you do it at night? And I wasn’t going to show myself on the bank during the day.”

“Well, that’s true. You had to stay in the woods all the time, of course. Did you hear them shooting the cannon?”

“Oh, yes. I knew they were after you. I saw them go by here—watched them through the bushes.

Some young birds flew along, flying a yard or two at a time and landing. Jim said it was a sign it was going to rain. He said it was a sign when young chickens flew that way, and so he thought it was the same when young birds did it. I wanted to catch some of them, but Jim wouldn’t let me. He said it was death. He said his father got very sick once, and someone caught a bird, and his grandmother said his father would die, and he did.

And Jim said you shouldn’t count the things you are going to cook for dinner, because that would bring bad luck. The same if you shook the tablecloth after sunset. And he said if a man owned a beehive and that man died, the bees must be told about it before sunrise the next morning, or else the bees would weaken and stop working and die. Jim said bees wouldn’t sting fools; but I didn’t believe that, because I had tried them many times myself, and they wouldn’t sting me.

I had heard about some of these things before, but not all of them. Jim knew all kinds of signs. He said he knew most everything. I said it looked to me like all the signs were about bad luck, and so I asked him if there weren’t any good-luck signs. He said:

“Very few—and they aren’t any use to a person. What would you want to know when good luck’s coming for? Want to keep it away?” And he said: “If you have hairy arms and a hairy chest, it’s a sign you’re going to be rich. Well, there’s some use in a sign like that, because it’s so far ahead. You see, maybe you have to be poor a long time first, and so you might get discouraged and kill yourself if you didn’t know by the sign that you’re going to be rich someday.”

“Do you have hairy arms and a hairy chest, Jim?”

“What’s the use of asking that question? Don’t you see I do?”

“Well, are you rich?”

“No, but I was rich once, and I’m going to be rich again.”

“Do you have hairy arms and a hairy chest, Jim?”

“What’s the use of asking that question? Don’t you see I do?”

“Well, are you rich?”

“No, but I was rich once, and I’m going to be rich again.”

Every night now, I used to sneak onto land around ten o'clock at some small town and buy ten to fifteen cents worth of flour, bacon, or other food to eat. Sometimes I'd grab a chicken that wasn't roosting comfortably and take it with me. Pap always said to take a chicken when you had the chance because if you didn't want it yourself, you could always find someone who did, and doing a good deed was never forgotten. I never saw Pap when he didn't want the chicken himself, but that's what he used to say anyway.

In the mornings before daylight, I'd sneak into cornfields and borrow a watermelon, a mushmelon, a pumpkin, or some fresh corn or similar stuff. Pap always said it wasn't wrong to borrow things if you planned to pay them back eventually; but the widow said it was just a fancy name for stealing, and no decent person would do it. Jim said he thought the widow was partly right and Pap was partly right; so the best way would be for us to pick out two or three things from the list and decide not to borrow them anymore—then he figured it wouldn't be wrong to borrow the others. So we talked it over one night, drifting down the river, trying to decide whether to give up watermelons, cantaloupes, mushmelons, or something else. But by daylight we had it all settled and decided to drop crabapples and persimmons. We hadn't felt right before that, but now everything was comfortable. I was glad the way it turned out too, because crabapples are never good, and persimmons wouldn't be ripe for two or three months yet.

We shot a waterfowl now and then that got up too early in the morning or stayed out too late at night. All things considered, we lived pretty well.

On the fifth night below St. Louis, we had a big storm after midnight, with a lot of thunder and lightning, and the rain poured down in a solid sheet. We stayed in the wigwam and let the raft take care of itself. When the lightning flashed, we could see a big straight river ahead and high, rocky bluffs on both sides. After a while, I said, 'Hey, Jim, look over there!' It was a steamboat that had crashed into a rock. We were drifting straight toward it. The lightning showed it clearly. It was leaning over, with part of its upper deck above water, and you could see every little chimney guy clean and clear, and a chair by the big bell, with an old slouch hat hanging on the back of it when the flashes came.

Well, it being late at night and stormy, and everything so mysterious, I felt just the way any other kid would have felt when I saw that wreck lying there so sad and lonely in the middle of the river. I wanted to get aboard and sneak around a bit, to see what was there. So I said:

'Let's land on it, Jim.'

But Jim was against it at first. He said:

'I don't want to go fooling around with no wreck.'

“I am, am I? Well, you answer me this: Didn’t you bring out the line in the canoe to get to the tow-head?”

“No, I didn’t. What tow-head? I haven’t seen any tow-head.”

“You haven’t seen a tow-head? Look here, didn’t the line come loose and the raft start heading down the river, leaving you and the canoe behind in the fog?”

“What fog?”

“Well, the fog—the fog that’s been around all night. And didn’t you yell, and didn’t I yell, until we got mixed up in the islands and one of us got lost and the other was just as good as lost, because he didn’t know where he was? And didn’t I crash into a bunch of those islands and have a terrible time and almost drown? Now isn’t that true, boss—isn’t it true? You answer me that.”

“Well, this is too much for me, Jim. I haven’t seen no fog, nor no islands, nor no trouble, nor nothing. I’ve been sitting here talking with you all night till you went to sleep about ten minutes ago, and I reckon I did the same. You couldn’t have gotten drunk in that time, so of course you’ve been dreaming.”

“Dang it, how am I supposed to dream all that in ten minutes?”

“Well, hang it all, you did dream it, because none of it happened.”

“But, Huck, it’s all just as clear to me as—”

“It doesn’t make no difference how clear it is; there ain’t nothing to it. I know, because I’ve been here all the time.”

Jim didn’t say anything for about five minutes, just sat there thinking it over. Then he said:

“Well, then, I reckon I did dream it, Huck; but dog my cats if it ain’t the strongest dream I ever had. And I haven’t ever had no dream before that’s tired me like this one.”

“Oh, well, that’s all right, because a dream does tire a body like everything sometimes. But this one was a stunner; tell me all about it, Jim.”

So Jim started in and told me the whole thing through, just as it happened, only he added a lot of extra details. Then he said he had to start interpreting it, because it was sent as a warning. He said the first tow-head stood for a man that would try to do us some good, but the current was another man that would get us away from him. The yells were warnings that would come to us every now and then, and if we didn’t try hard to understand them, they’d just lead us into bad luck instead of keeping us out of it. The bunch of tow-heads was trouble we were going to get into with quarrelsome people and all kinds of mean folks, but if we minded our business and didn’t argue back and aggravate them, we would pull through and get out of the fog and into the big clear river, which was the free States, and wouldn’t have no more trouble.

It had gotten pretty dark just after I got on the raft, but it was clearing up again now.

“Oh, well, that’s all interpreted well enough as far as it goes, Jim,” I said; “but what do these things stand for?”
