The residents had already left some of them. The bank had collapsed under one corner of others, and that corner was about to fall in. People still lived in those houses, but it was risky, because sometimes a strip of land as wide as a house would collapse at once. Sometimes a stretch of land a quarter-mile deep would begin to cave in and keep going until it all tumbled into the river in a single summer. A town like that had to keep moving back and back and back, because the river was always wearing it away.

The closer it got to noon that day, the more wagons and horses filled the streets, and more kept coming all the time. Country folks brought their lunches and ate them in the wagons. There was a fair amount of drinking going on, and I saw three fights. Then someone shouted out:

“Here comes old Boggs!—he’s in town for his monthly little spree; here he comes, boys!”

All the idlers looked pleased; I figured they were used to getting amusement from Boggs. One of them said:

“Wonder who he’s going to chew out this time. If he’d chewed out all the men he’s been going to chew out in the last twenty years, he’d have quite a reputation now.”

Another one said, “I wish old Boggs would threaten me, ’cause then I’d know I wasn’t going to die for a thousand years.”

Boggs came tearing along on his horse, whooping and yelling like an Indian, and shouting:

“Clear the track, there. I’m on the war-path, and the price of coffins is going to rise.”

He was drunk and swaying in his saddle; he was over fifty years old, and had a very red face. Everyone yelled at him and laughed at him and teased him, and he teased back, and said he’d take care of them and lay them out in their turn, but he couldn’t wait now because he’d come to town to kill old Colonel Sherburn, and his motto was, “Meat first, and spoon vittles to top off on.”

He saw me, and rode up and said:

“Where’d you come from, boy? You ready to die?”

Then he rode on. I was scared, but a man said:

“He don’t mean nothing; he’s always carrying on like that when he’s drunk. He’s the best-natured old fool in Arkansas—never hurt nobody, drunk or sober.”

Boggs rode up in front of the biggest store in town, and bent his head down so he could see under the curtain of the awning and yelled:

“Come out here, Sherburn! Come out and meet the man you’ve swindled. You’re the hound I’m after, and I’m going to get you, too!”

And so he went on, calling Sherburn every name he could think of, and the whole street packed with people listening and laughing and carrying on. By-and-by a proud-looking man about fifty-five—and he was the best-dressed man in that town, too—stepped out of the store, and the crowd dropped back on each side to let him come. He said to Boggs, very calm and slow—he said:

“I’m tired of this, but I’ll put up with it till one o’clock.”

He kept walking around, talking a lot and enjoying the sound of his own voice. Every now and then, he brought up the topic of funeral ceremonies again. Eventually, the duke couldn’t take it anymore. He wrote on a small piece of paper, ‘_obsequies_, you old fool,’ folded it up, and passed it over people’s heads to him. The king read it, put it in his pocket, and said:

He stood up and looked out the window. The sunset had turned the windows of the houses across the street a deep red gold. The glass looked like hot metal. The sky above was the color of a faded rose. He thought about his friend’s young, passionate life and wondered how it would all end.

When he got home, around half past twelve, he saw a telegram on the hall table. He opened it and saw it was from Dorian Gray. It said he was going to be married to Sibyl Vane.


CHAPTER V.


“Mother, Mother, I’m so happy!” the girl whispered, hiding her face in the lap of the older, tired-looking woman who sat in the only armchair in their small, shabby room. “I’m so happy!” she said again. “And you must be happy too!”

Mrs. Vane winced and placed her pale, white-powdered hands on her daughter’s head. “Happy?” she repeated. “I’m only happy when I see you act. You must think only about your acting. Mr. Isaacs has been very kind to us, and we owe him money.”

The girl looked up and pouted. “Money, Mother?” she said. “What does money matter? Love is more than money.”

“Mr. Isaacs gave us fifty pounds to pay our debts and to get a proper outfit for James. You must not forget that, Sibyl. Fifty pounds is a lot. Mr. Isaacs has been very generous.”

“He isn’t a gentleman, Mother, and I hate the way he talks to me,” the girl said, standing up and walking to the window.

“I don’t know how we could manage without him,” the older woman replied, sounding upset.

Sibyl Vane shook her head and laughed. “We don’t need him anymore, Mother. Prince Charming is in charge of our lives now.” Then she stopped. A rose bloomed in her cheeks. Her breath came quickly, like petals parting. Her lips trembled. A warm wind of passion moved through her and lifted the soft folds of her dress. “I love him,” she said simply.

“Foolish child! Foolish child!” the mother said, repeating the words. Her thin fingers, decorated with fake jewels, waved in the air, making the words seem silly.

The girl laughed again. Her voice sounded like the joy of a bird in a cage. Her eyes caught the sound and reflected it in light, then closed for a moment as if to hide something. When they opened, a dream had passed over them.

From the worn chair came a voice, thin and full of caution, offering advice and quoting the book of common sense. She didn’t listen. She felt free in her prison of passion. Her prince, Prince Charming, was with her. She had asked memory to bring him back. She had sent her soul to find him, and it had returned with him. His kiss burned again on her lips. Her eyelids were warm with his breath.

Then the voice changed and spoke of secrets and being discovered. This young man might be rich. If so, marriage should be considered. Against the side of her ear came the waves of worldly cleverness.

He was supposed to get off the ship in Melbourne, say a polite goodbye to the captain, and head straight to the goldfields. Within a week, he was going to discover a huge chunk of pure gold, the biggest ever found, and bring it down to the coast in a wagon guarded by six armed police on horseback. The bushrangers were going to attack them three times and be badly beaten each time. Or, no. He wasn’t going to go to the goldfields at all. They were terrible places where men got drunk, shot each other in bars, and used bad language. He was supposed to be a nice sheep farmer, and one evening, while riding home, he would see the beautiful heiress being kidnapped by a robber on a black horse, chase after her, and rescue her. Of course, she would fall in love with him, and he with her, and they would get married and live in a huge house in London. Yes, there were great things in store for him. But he had to be really good, not lose his temper, or spend his money foolishly. She was only a year older than him, but she knew so much more about life. He also had to make sure to write to her with every mail and say his prayers each night before going to sleep. God was really good and would look out for him. She would pray for him too, and in a few years he would come back rich and happy.

The boy listened sulkily and didn’t say a word. He was heartbroken about leaving home.

But it wasn’t just that which made him gloomy and moody. Even though he was inexperienced, he had a strong sense of the danger Sibyl was in. This young guy who was flirting with her wasn’t going to do her any good. He was a gentleman, and he hated him for that, hated him for some strange instinct he couldn’t explain, and because of that, it was even stronger inside him. He also realized how shallow and vain his mother was, and in that, he saw a huge threat to Sibyl and her happiness. Kids start by loving their parents; as they get older, they judge them; sometimes they forgive them.

His mother! He had something on his mind he wanted to ask her, something he had been thinking about for months of silence. A random comment he had overheard at the theater, a whispered sneer that had reached his ears one night while he was waiting at the stage door, had triggered a series of terrible thoughts. He remembered it as if it had been a whip across his face. His eyebrows furrowed into a deep frown, and with a twitch of pain, he bit his lower lip.

“You’re not listening to a word I’m saying, Jim,” Sibyl said, “and I’m making the most wonderful plans for your future. Do say something.”

“What do you want me to say?”

“Oh! That you’ll be a good boy and not forget us,” she replied, smiling at him.

He shrugged. “You’re more likely to forget me than I am to forget you, Sibyl.”

“Pleasure is the only thing worth having a theory about,” he answered in his slow, smooth voice. “But I’m afraid I can’t claim the theory as my own. It belongs to Nature, not me. Pleasure is Nature’s test, her sign of approval. When we’re happy, we’re always good, but when we’re good, we’re not always happy.”

“Ah! But what do you mean by good?” cried Basil Hallward.

“Yes,” echoed Dorian, leaning back in his chair and looking at Lord Henry over the heavy clusters of purple-lipped irises that stood in the center of the table, “what do you mean by good, Harry?”

“To be good is to be in harmony with yourself,” he replied, tapping the thin stem of his glass with his pale, fine-pointed fingers. “Discord is being forced to be in harmony with others. Your own life—that’s the important thing. As for the lives of your neighbors, if you want to be a prig or a Puritan, you can go on about your moral views, but they’re not your concern. Besides, individualism has the higher aim. Modern morality is just about accepting the standard of your age. I think it’s the grossest immorality for any cultured man to accept the standard of his time.”

“But, surely, if you live only for yourself, Harry, you pay a terrible price for it?” suggested the painter.

“Yes, we’re overcharged for everything these days. I’d say the real tragedy of the poor is that they can’t afford anything but self-denial. Beautiful sins, like beautiful things, are the privilege of the rich.”

“One has to pay in other ways besides money.”

“What sort of ways, Basil?”

“Oh! I’d say in remorse, in suffering, in ... well, in the feeling of being degraded.”

Lord Henry shrugged. “My dear fellow, medieval art is charming, but medieval emotions are out of date. You can use them in fiction, of course. But the only things you can use in fiction are the things you’ve stopped using in real life. Believe me, no civilized man ever regrets a pleasure, and no uncivilized man ever knows what a pleasure is.”

“I know what pleasure is,” cried Dorian Gray. “It’s to adore someone.”

“That’s certainly better than being adored,” he answered, playing with some fruit. “Being adored is a pain. Women treat us just like humanity treats its gods. They worship us and are always bugging us to do something for them.”

“I’d have thought that whatever they ask for, they’ve given to us first,” murmured the young man seriously. “They create love in our lives. They have a right to expect it back.”

“That’s absolutely true, Dorian,” cried Hallward.

“Nothing is ever absolutely true,” said Lord Henry.

“This is,” interrupted Dorian. “You have to admit, Harry, that women give men the very best of themselves.”

“Possibly,” he sighed, “but they always want it back in tiny pieces. That’s the problem. Women, as some clever Frenchman once said, inspire us with the desire to do masterpieces and always stop us from doing them.”

“Harry, you’re terrible! I don’t know why I like you so much.”

And yet, the thing would still live on. It would always be alive.

He shivered, and for a moment he wished he had told Basil the real reason he wanted to hide the painting. Basil would have helped him resist Lord Henry's influence and the even worse influence from his own nature. The love he felt for Basil—because it really was love—was noble and intellectual. It wasn't just a physical admiration of beauty that comes from the senses and fades when the senses get tired. It was the kind of love Michelangelo, Montaigne, Winckelmann, and Shakespeare himself had known. Yes, Basil could have saved him. But now it was too late. The past could always be erased. Regret, denial, or forgetfulness could do that. But the future was unavoidable. There were passions in him that would find their terrible release, and dreams that would make the shadow of their evil real.

He picked up the large purple-and-gold fabric that covered the couch and, holding it in his hands, went behind the screen. Was the face on the canvas worse than before? It seemed unchanged to him, and yet his hatred of it had grown. Golden hair, blue eyes, and rose-red lips—they were all still there. It was just the expression that had changed. That was cruel and horrifying. Compared to what he saw in it of blame or criticism, how shallow Basil's complaints about Sibyl Vane had been!—how shallow, and how unimportant! His own soul was looking out at him from the canvas and calling him to judgment. A look of pain crossed his face, and he threw the rich cloth over the painting. As he did, a knock came at the door. He left the room just as his servant entered.

“The men are here, Monsieur.”

He felt the man had to be sent away right away. He couldn't be allowed to know where the painting was being taken. There was something sneaky about him, and he had thoughtful, treacherous eyes. Sitting at the writing desk, he quickly wrote a note to Lord Henry, asking him to send something to read and reminding him they were to meet at eight-fifteen that evening.

“Wait for an answer,” he said, handing it to the servant, “and show the men in here.”

In two or three minutes, there was another knock, and Mr. Hubbard himself, the famous frame-maker from South Audley Street, came in with a somewhat rough-looking young assistant. Mr. Hubbard was a red-faced, red-whiskered little man whose love for art was often mixed with the constant financial struggles of most of the artists who dealt with him. Usually, he never left his shop. He waited for people to come to him. But he always made an exception for Dorian Gray. There was something about Dorian that charmed everyone. It was a pleasure even to see him.

“What can I do for you, Mr. Gray?” he asked, rubbing his fat, freckled hands. “I thought I'd do myself the honor of coming round in person. I just got a beautiful frame, sir. Found it at a sale.”

There was a terrible allure to them all. He saw them at night, and they haunted his thoughts in the day. The Renaissance was familiar with peculiar methods of poisoning—poisoning by a helmet and a lit torch, by an embroidered glove and a jeweled fan, by a gilded pomander and an amber chain. Dorian Gray had been poisoned by a book. There were times when he regarded evil merely as a means through which he could express his vision of beauty.

It was on the ninth of November, the night before his thirty-eighth birthday, as he often recalled later.

He was returning home about eleven o’clock from Lord Henry’s, where he had dined, and was wrapped in thick furs, as the night was cold and foggy. “Dorian! What an extraordinary coincidence! I’ve been waiting for you in your library since nine o’clock. Eventually, I took pity on your exhausted servant and told him to go to bed, as he let me out.”
